brief_summary:
Why is this study being done? Nurses in the emergency department often need to place a thin plastic tube, called an IV catheter, into a vein in the arm. The tube is used to give medicines and fluids. For some patients this is hard because veins are hard to see or feel. Nurses may need to try more than once, which can hurt and delay treatment.

Ultrasound is a tool that uses sound waves to make a live picture of the veins under the skin. Nurses can use the picture to guide the needle. Earlier research suggests that ultrasound may help nurses place the tube on the first try in patients with hard-to-find veins. More research is needed, especially on nurses working in emergency departments.

This is a small pilot study. A pilot study is a first, smaller study that tests an idea before a larger study is planned. It was done as part of a nursing degree thesis project.

The main question is: do adults with hard-to-find veins get the IV tube placed on the first try more often with ultrasound than with the usual method? The usual method is to look at the arm and feel for a vein.

The study also looks at:

* how many tries are needed
* how long it takes to place the tube
* problems right after placement, such as bruising or fluid leaking out of the vein
* how much pain patients feel
* how satisfied patients are with the procedure

Who can join? Adults age 18 or older who come to the emergency department, need an IV tube, and are likely to have hard-to-find veins. At triage (the first check on arrival), nurses use a short checklist called the ea-DIVA score to find these patients. A score of 8 or more out of 11 means that veins are likely to be hard to find.

Patients cannot join when emergency care is needed right away, when pain is strong and uncontrolled, when an IV tube cannot be placed in the arm (for example because of swelling, infection, or a dialysis connection), when a central line (a longer tube placed in a large vein) is urgently needed, when consent cannot be given, or when no nurse trained in ultrasound is available.

What happens to participants? Participants are placed by chance, using a computer-made random list, in one of two groups. The group is marked on the wristband at triage.

* Ultrasound group: the nurse uses ultrasound to find the vein and guide the needle.
* Usual method group: the nurse looks and feels for a vein. If two tries do not work, the nurse switches to ultrasound.

Participants are not told in advance which group was assigned, but may notice the technique during the procedure. The study team records the number of tries, the time needed, and any problems. After the procedure, participants rate pain from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain) and satisfaction from 0 (not satisfied) to 10 (very satisfied). Taking part lasts only as long as the IV placement. There are no follow-up visits.

What are the possible benefits and risks? Participants may get the IV tube with fewer tries and less waiting, but this is not guaranteed. The risks are the same as for any IV tube: pain, bruising, fluid leaking out of the vein, or the tube moving out of place. Ultrasound does not use radiation.

Taking part is voluntary. Patients can decline or stop at any time, and care does not change. Written consent is obtained.

Where is the study? The study took place in the emergency department of a university hospital in Italy.
primary_outcomes: first-attempt insertion success rate
title: Effectiveness of Ultrasound-Guided Placement of Peripheral Venous Access in Adult Patients With Difficult Intravenous Access (DIVA)

brief_summary: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major global public health challenge. It often causes no obvious symptoms in the early stage, so most patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage. This highlights the importance of gastric cancer screening among high-risk populations to achieve early detection and improve survival outcomes. People infected with Helicobacter pylori (Hp) are at high risk of gastric cancer. Hp is one of the most common bacterial infections worldwide. It initiates carcinogenesis by triggering chronic atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia, known as the Correa cascade. However, the acceptance of gastric cancer screening among Hp-infected individuals is still unsatisfactory. To our knowledge, there are few theory-based interventions designed to help Hp-infected people make decisions about gastric cancer screening and increase screening uptake. Therefore, based on our previous systematic review, this study aims to develop a health promotion program to improve gastric cancer screening participation among Hp-infected individuals in mainland China. Participants in the intervention group will receive a comprehensive health promotion program, including a 30-minute health education session. They will receive a 15-minute telephone follow-up with gastric cancer screening information in week 2, and additional 10-minute telephone follow-ups at weeks 2, 4, and 6 to help participants identify and overcome barriers to gastric cancer screening. Participants in the control group will receive routine care. Data on gastric cancer screening participation will be collected at the end of the intervention. Findings from this study will be valuable for gastric cancer prevention among people with Hp infection.
interventions: Health Belief Model-based screening promotion intervention
primary_outcomes: Gastric cancer screening intention
Gastroscopy completion rate
title: Development of a Gastric Cancer Screening Intervention for H. Pylori Carriers Based on the Health Belief Model

brief_summary:
The goal of this observational study is to learn whether measurements of bile duct and duodenal anatomy on a routine pre-operative MRCP scan (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, an MRI of the bile and pancreatic ducts) can predict difficult bile duct cannulation during ERCP in adults with gallbladder stones and bile duct stones who are treated in a single operation called laparoendoscopic rendezvous.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Can a score calculated only from the MRCP scan predict which patients will have difficult cannulation, as defined by European guideline criteria?
* Which anatomical features, such as the angle at which the bile duct meets the duodenum, a pouch (diverticulum) next to the papilla, or a stone wedged at the lower end of the bile duct, are linked to difficult cannulation, and how reliably can radiologists measure them?
* Would using the score to decide when to pass the rendezvous wire first be more useful than passing it in every patient or in none?

The researchers expect that anatomy measured on the MRCP scan alone, without any clinical or blood-test information, will predict difficult cannulation well enough to guide when the rendezvous wire should be used first.

Participants already scheduled for laparoendoscopic rendezvous as part of their regular medical care will:

* Have their routine pre-operative MRCP measured by two radiologists who do not know what happened during the operation.
* Undergo the planned operation, in which the gallbladder is removed by keyhole surgery and, during the same anesthetic, the endoscopist first tries to enter the bile duct through the papilla (its small opening into the duodenum) within fixed time and attempt limits. If those limits are reached, the surgeon passes a guidewire from above, through the cystic duct and out through the papilla, which makes entry easy (the rendezvous wire). Higher-risk rescue techniques are not used before the rendezvous wire.
* Receive the guideline-recommended anti-inflammatory suppository that lowers the risk of pancreatitis after ERCP.
* Have blood tests 4 and 24 hours after the procedure and attend follow-up at 30 and 90 days.

Difficult cannulation is the main procedural cause of pancreatitis after ERCP and of failed stone clearance. The rendezvous wire can prevent it, but it is currently used either in every patient or only after difficulty has already occurred. A score calculated from the scan before surgery could allow the wire to be used first in the patients who need it. The study does not change any treatment decision, and the score will need testing in other hospitals before it is used in routine care.
interventions: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) with structured blinded morphometry
Single-stage laparoendoscopic rendezvous with a standardized, capped cannulation phase
primary_outcomes: Difficult biliary cannulation of the native papilla (ESGE composite definition)
title: Using MRCP Anatomy to Predict Difficult Bile Duct Cannulation During Single-Stage Laparoendoscopic Rendezvous for Gallbladder and Bile Duct Stones

brief_summary:
This study aims to investigate the comparative effect of visual versus auditory support on communication skills in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Communication impairments are a core feature of ASD and significantly impact children's social interaction, academic participation, and daily functioning. Although visual-based strategies and auditory-based strategies are widely used in speech-language therapy, there is limited experimental evidence directly comparing their effectiveness. Therefore, this study seeks to determine which support modality results in greater improvement in expressive and receptive communication skills in children with ASD, providing evidence-based guidance for speech-language pathologists.A randomized controlled trial design will be employed using convenience sampling. The study will recruit a total of 24 children diagnosed with mild to moderate ASD, aged 4-12 years, from PSN School, PAF Base Lahore. Participants will be randomly assigned into two equal groups, with 12 children in each group. Group A (Visual Support Group) will receive visual communication interventions, including PECS.

Group B (Auditory Support Group)will receive auditory-based communication interventions, such as verbal prompts \& auditory cues
interventions: Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS) guide and Checklist
primary_outcomes: Visual Tool Test Checklist and Auditory Processing Difficulties Checklist
title: Effects of Visual Versus Auditory Supports on Communication of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)

brief_summary:
This is a randomized controlled trial. The study population consists of a minimum of 162 Primary Health Care professionals. The sample includes physicians, nurses, nursing technicians, and nursing assistants involved in direct patient care at selected Primary Health Care Units who agree to participate in the study.

The Primary Health Care Units were stratified according to size and randomly allocated into two groups. Health professionals from these units were invited to participate either in the intervention group (n=81) or the control group (n=81). Participants in the intervention group will receive escape room-based training, whereas participants in the control group will receive traditional training through a dialogic lecture. Due to the nature of the intervention, neither participants nor the principal investigator will be blinded.

Both groups will be assessed regarding Basic Life Support (BLS) knowledge and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) skills at three time points: baseline before training (T0), immediately after training (T1), and 15 days after training (T2).

Objective - To evaluate whether escape room-based training for the management of cardiopulmonary arrest (CPA) among Primary Health Care professionals is effective in improving the retention of CPR knowledge and skills when compared with traditional dialogic lecture-based training.
interventions: Audiovisual simulation training and educational escape room
primary_outcomes: Knowledge Test
Skills Test
title: THE ESCAPE ROOM FOR CARDIORESPIRATORY ARREST CARE IN PRIMARY HEALTH CARE

brief_summary:
This study will evaluate the effects of the UTI Biome Shield capsule on urinary symptoms in sexually active women aged 18-45 who experience recurrent symptoms associated with urinary tract infections (UTIs). The trial is a single-arm, unblinded, virtual study conducted over six months, in which all 44 enrolled participants will use the test product daily.

Participants will complete questionnaires at Baseline and at the end of Months 1 through 6. The primary objective is to examine the product's effects on urinary symptoms, while secondary objectives assess participants' perceptions of the product's effects, including reduced recurrence of UTI-associated symptoms in sexually active women and reduced recurrence of symptoms after sex.
primary_outcomes: Change in Urinary Symptoms
title: A Clinical Trial to Evaluate the Effects of a Supplement on Urinary Symptoms

brief_summary:
This is a single-group, open-label, decentralized clinical trial evaluating the effects of 12 weeks of once-daily consumption of Glow Shakes Premium Collagen Meal Replacement on nutritional adequacy, body composition, skin health, satiety, and overall wellness in 40 adults aged 18-55 years who are currently using a GLP-1 receptor agonist or dual-incretin medication for weight management. All study activities are conducted remotely; participants complete questionnaire assessments and smart scale body composition measurements at home at Baseline, Week 4, Week 8, and Week 12.

Participants replace a typical meal once daily with the study product for 12 consecutive weeks while continuing their existing GLP-1 or dual-incretin medication. The primary objective is to evaluate within-participant change in perceived nutritional adequacy from Baseline to Week 12. Secondary objectives include changes in body fat percentage, muscle mass, perceived skin health, hunger and satiety, hair health, energy and cognitive focus, nail health, gut comfort, metabolism support, physical strength, and product tolerability and satisfaction.
interventions: Glow Shakes Premium Collagen Meal Replacement Intervention
primary_outcomes: Change in Perceived Nutritional Adequacy
title: A Clinical Trial to Evaluate the Effects of Glow Shakes Premium Collagen Meal Replacement on Nutritional Adequacy, Body Composition, Skin Health, Satiety, and Overall Wellness in Adults Using GLP-1 or Dual-Incretin Medications for Weight Management
